parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman phones a language school to enrol on an evening course.
script: Good evening, Ridgeway Language Centre, Daniel speaking. How can I help?
Oh, hello. I'm hoping to enrol on one of your evening courses, if there are still places. I've been looking at the autumn programme on your website.
Yes, we've got quite a few courses starting next month. Which language were you interested in?
Italian. My partner and I are going to Sicily next summer, and I'd like to be able to do a bit more than just order coffee.
Lovely. We run Italian at three different levels. Have you studied it before?
Only a little, years ago at school, so I think I'd count as a beginner.
Then Italian for Beginners is the one you want. Let me just take some details. Can I have your name, please?
Could you spell the surname for me?
Of course. It's L-I-N-D-Q-V-I-S-T. People always leave out the Q.
Thanks. Now, the beginners' class used to meet on Tuesdays, but that's changed. At the moment it's on Wednesday evenings, and there are still seven places left.
Wednesday would be fine. Tuesday would actually have been tricky for me, because I sing in a choir. What time does it start?
Well, our old timetable said seven o'clock, but it now starts at 6.30 and finishes at 8.30, so there's a short break halfway through.
6.30 is perfect. I finish work at five, so that gives me time to get home and have something to eat. And when does the course begin?
Let me see. The leaflet says the 7th of October, but that's a misprint, I'm afraid. The first lesson is on the 14th of October, and the course runs for ten weeks.
Right, the 14th of October. And what's the fee?
For the ten weeks it's 185 pounds. We do have an intensive version at 210 pounds, but that means two evenings a week, and I don't think you'd want that.
No, one evening is plenty. Does that price include the books?

Not quite. Everybody gets the handouts free of charge, but you'll need to buy the workbook from our shop. It's about 12 pounds. You don't have to buy the textbook as well, because we've found that most people never open it.
Good to know. I'll pick up the workbook on the first night, then.
That's fine. Now, can I take your address?
ST4 8JN. Thank you. Now, how would you like to pay?
Can I pay in cash when I come in for the first lesson?
I'm afraid we stopped taking cash in the summer. You can pay by card online, or you can make a bank transfer.
I'd rather not put my card details on a website, so bank transfer, please. I'll do it tonight if you can send me the account number.
Of course. I'll email it to you within the hour, together with a map showing how to find the building. It's just behind the old cinema.
And one last question, which we ask everyone. How did you hear about the school?
A colleague of mine did the Spanish course here last year, and she couldn't stop talking about it. I did look at your website as well, but it was her recommendation that made up my mind.
That's nice to hear. Well, Karina, you're all registered. We look forward to seeing you on the 14th, and good luck with the Italian.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: The manager of a new student residence describes the facilities and rules to new residents.
script: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Kingsfield Hall. My name's Rosa Tane and I'm the residence manager. Before you collect your keys, I'd like to spend ten minutes or so telling you about the building and a few house rules.

First, some background. Kingsfield Hall opened only three weeks ago, so you are among the very first students to live here. When the university drew up the plans, the building was meant to house 200 students. During construction, an extra floor was added, and we now have room for 240. Forty of those places are reserved for postgraduates, who live on the fourth floor, but everyone shares the same facilities.

You may have read in the brochure that the building is heated by solar panels. I'm afraid that's out of date. The roof turned out to be too shaded by the library next door, so the panels were never fitted. Instead, the hot water comes from the heat that is collected from the swimming pool at the sports centre across the road.

Now for the rules, and there are only a few. Visitors are welcome, but every guest has to be registered at reception when they arrive, and they must leave by ten at night. Overnight stays were suggested, but the residents' committee voted against them. Quiet hours are the next thing. The original proposal was ten o'clock on weekdays and midnight at weekends, but students said that was too complicated to remember. So, quiet hours begin at 11 every night, and I'd ask you to respect that, particularly during the exam period.

Let me move on to the facilities. I'll take them in the order that people usually ask me about them. The first is the gym. It was originally planned for the basement, but there were problems with the ceiling height, so it ended up on the first floor, at the end of the corridor on the left. It's open from six in the morning until ten at night, and it's free for residents.
Next, the bike store. The store used to be in the basement, but it's now at the back of the building on the ground floor, behind reception, and you open it with the same card as your front door.

We have three music practice rooms, and these are very popular. They're on the second floor. There was a plan to put them on the third floor, but the soundproofing would have been too expensive, so they sit right above the common room.

Then there's the laundry. Unlike in some of the older halls, there are no washing machines on each floor. Everything is together in the basement. There are twelve machines and eight dryers, and you pay with your student card.
If you need somewhere quiet to work, the study lounge is on the third floor. It has big tables, plenty of sockets and a rule that no one talks above a whisper.

Finally, my favourite, the roof terrace. Get a key from reception, and you can use it from eight in the morning until ten at night. There are tables and benches and a wonderful view of the harbour. Barbecues are not allowed, I'm afraid, because of the fire regulations, but you're welcome to bring a picnic.
That's everything from me for now. The rest of the rules are in your information pack. Now, if you'd like to line up, we'll hand out the keys.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students discuss their fieldwork report on coastal erosion.
script: Right, Dana, shall we go through our coastal erosion report? I've printed the draft, and we've only got until Friday.
Okay. I've read it twice, and I think it's in decent shape, but a few things worry me.
Same here. Let's start with the big picture. Do you think we've explained why we picked Marram Bay?
Partly. We said it was easy to get to, but to be fair it took two buses and a long walk, so that isn't much of a reason.
True. And it isn't the fastest eroding cliff in the region either. That's Seaton Point, but the council closed it after the rockfall.

Right. The real reason is that the coastal authority has been measuring Marram Bay every year since 1998. Having those records meant we could compare our own figures with theirs, and I think that's the point we should make.
Agreed. Now, the fieldwork itself. I've mentioned the tide problem on the second day, but only in one sentence.
Oh, that was a pain. We'd checked the tables and thought we had until three o'clock, but the water came in an hour earlier, and we couldn't get round the headland to the last site.
Yes, and I'd rather say so honestly than pretend we measured it. At least nothing broke, and the equipment was fine.
It was. We calibrated it before we left. No, my real worry is something else. We only went in October. Erosion is much worse after the winter storms, so our figures might look too low.
Hmm, that's a fair point. I'd been more worried about having five sites rather than ten, but with a two-day trip that was all we could manage.
I think the sites are fine. It's the single visit I'd mention.
Okay. What about the graphs? I like the bar charts, but a reader can't tell which cliff is which.
They are a bit confusing. Should we switch to line graphs?
I don't think so. Bars are fine for five sites. But we should label each one with the type of rock, clay or sandstone, because that's what explains the differences.
Good idea. I'll do that this evening.
Now, how should we split up the rest? I could take the first half and you take the second, and then we swap?
Honestly, I'd rather sit down together on Thursday and go through everything in one go. Last time we did it separately, we ended up contradicting each other.
Fair enough. Thursday afternoon in the library, then.
So, section by section. The introduction. We agreed it's far too long. Two pages before we even mention the cliffs.
Then we cut it down to one page. It's the easiest fix.
The text about the stakes is clear enough, but I had to read it twice to see where they were placed. A diagram of the layout would solve that.
I can sketch the three lines of stakes and scan it in.
Perfect. Now the results. I noticed the retreat figure for site three is 1.2 metres in the table but 2.1 in the text. One of them must be a typo.
I'll check them both against our notebooks. It would be terrible to lose marks over a slip like that.
And the discussion. Honestly, it reads like a list of facts. I think it needs to be written again from scratch, with the argument first and the details afterwards.
Should we ask Dr Okoye to look at it before we start?
She's away until Monday, so there's no point. We'll rewrite it ourselves.
That's actually the best part. I wouldn't touch it.
Agreed. We'll leave it as it is, and spend the time on the discussion.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on the invention of paper and how it spread across the world.
script: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to look at an object that is so common we hardly notice it: paper.

Let's start with a simple question. What did people write on before paper? The answer depends on where you lived. In Mesopotamia they used clay tablets, in Egypt they used papyrus made from reeds, and in Europe they used parchment made from animal skin. In China, writers used strips of bamboo. Bamboo is cheap, but a long document was extremely heavy. The alternative was silk, which was light and pleasant to write on but very expensive, so only the richest people could afford it. Clearly, there was a need for something cheaper and lighter.

According to Chinese tradition, that need was met by a court official named Cai Lun, who presented the emperor with a sheet of paper in the year 105. Archaeologists have found older fragments, so Cai Lun probably improved the process rather than inventing it. But his recipe is well documented. He mixed the inner bark of trees with hemp, rags and old fishing nets, soaked the mixture and pounded it into a pulp. Some later sources mention silk waste as an ingredient, but that was unusual.

For several centuries, papermaking stayed inside China, and then it began to travel east. Paper was being made in Korea by the fourth century. From there, a Korean monk is said to have carried the technique to Japan, in about the year 610.

The journey west was much slower, and it depended on a historical accident. The Chinese kept papermaking a closely guarded secret. What changed matters was a battle in 751, fought beside the Talas river in Central Asia. That's spelled T-A-L-A-S. An Arab army defeated a Chinese force there, and among the prisoners were skilled papermakers. They were taken to the city of Samarkand, and under their direction Samarkand became the first great papermaking centre outside China.

The technology then moved quickly. By the year 794, a mill had opened in Baghdad, and this one was built to supply paper for government documents. That was a significant moment. Until then, the administrators of the Islamic world had relied on papyrus, whose supply from Egypt was unreliable, and on parchment, which was costly. Cheap paper made it possible to run a large bureaucracy.

Christian Europe, however, was slow to adopt paper. Parchment had a long tradition, and some authorities were suspicious of paper because it was made by Muslims and was thought to be less durable. Yet by the thirteenth century, Italian mills, especially those around the town of Fabriano, had introduced two important improvements. First, the mills used water to drive heavy hammers that beat the rags into pulp, a job that had previously been done by hand or by animals. Second, they began to add watermarks, a design pressed into the sheet which showed which mill had produced the paper. The invention of printing in the 1450s then created an enormous demand.

That demand brought a new problem in the nineteenth century. Paper was made from old cloth, and there simply weren't enough rags to go round. Papermakers tried straw and grass, but the real solution was to make paper from wood pulp.
So the invention of paper was not a single moment but a long process of improvement and borrowing, shaped by war, trade and the needs of governments. Are there any questions?

passages.title: How birds find their way
paras: A  Every autumn, billions of birds leave their breeding grounds and head for warmer places, and every spring most of them come back. The scale of some journeys is hard to believe. The Arctic tern, a bird weighing about as much as a bar of soap, travels from the northern edge of the world to the Antarctic seas and back again, a round trip of some 70,000 kilometres. Even more puzzling is the fact that many species make their first migration alone. Young cuckoos, for example, are raised by foster parents of another species, and their real parents leave weeks before them, yet they reach the right part of Africa with no one to show them the way. For more than a century, scientists have asked how birds manage this. The answer, it turns out, is not a single trick but a collection of tools, which birds combine in different ways.

B  The first tool to be understood was the sun. In the 1950s, the ornithologist Matthias Roder placed starlings in a circular cage with windows around its sides. Whenever the birds felt the urge to migrate, they fluttered towards the same point of the compass, but when Roder used mirrors to shift the apparent position of the sun, they changed direction by the same angle. The sun moves across the sky during the day, so a bird can only steer by it if it knows what time it is. Roder's colleague Elsa Brandt showed that birds do possess an internal clock of this kind. She kept starlings in rooms where the lights came on six hours later than natural dawn. When the birds were then tested in the cage, they set off about ninety degrees away from the correct direction, exactly as would be expected if their sense of time had been shifted by six hours.

C  The sun is no help at night, and many small birds, such as warblers and buntings, migrate in the dark. A team led by Dr Ingrid Solheim at the Marlow Institute therefore raised young buntings in a planetarium. One group saw a normal night sky, which slowly rotated around the pole star as the real sky does. A second group saw a sky that rotated around Betelgeuse, a bright star in a different part of the heavens. A third group never saw any stars at all. When autumn came, the first group set off in the correct direction. The second group behaved as if Betelgeuse marked true north. The third group could not use the stars, although they found their way perfectly well when they were given a magnetic field to follow. The star compass, then, is not inherited. Birds must learn it by looking up when they are young. What seems to be inherited is the ability to learn.

D  A third compass is the hardest for humans to imagine, because we have no sense of it. The Earth is surrounded by a magnetic field, and birds such as the European robin can detect it. Robins placed inside a coil of wires changed the direction in which they hopped whenever the field was artificially rotated. How they detect it is still debated. One theory proposes that special light-sensitive proteins in the eye are affected by the field, allowing the bird to see a pattern across its vision. A rival theory proposes that tiny particles of iron in the beak act as miniature compass needles. These particles were once thought to be the answer, but later studies showed that they lay in cells of the immune system rather than in nerves. Most researchers now consider the eye theory the more promising, though few would claim that the question has been settled.

E  A compass tells a bird which way to fly; it does not tell it where it is. For that, it needs a map. The best evidence for such a map comes from displacement experiments. In one, researchers caught several hundred migrating starlings, both adults and juveniles, moved them about 1,000 kilometres to the west and released them. The juveniles continued to fly in the same compass direction as before, and ended up far to the west of where they should have been. The adults, by contrast, appeared to recognise that they had been moved and corrected their course, heading towards their usual wintering area. Experience, then, seems to build a map in the bird's brain. What the map is made of remains uncertain. Some seabirds appear to follow smells, and homing pigeons with blocked nostrils find their way home much less reliably. Others may listen to infrasound, the very low-frequency sound produced by distant ocean waves and mountains, which can travel for hundreds of kilometres. Visual landmarks such as coastlines and rivers also help, especially near the end of a journey.

F  Our understanding is growing quickly, and the main reason is technology. Until recently, tracking devices were too heavy for songbirds. Today, light-level loggers weighing less than a gram can be fitted to a bird's back, recording the times of dawn and dusk, from which its position can be calculated. When the bird is recaptured a year later, the data are downloaded, and they have revealed journeys that nobody suspected. The same research has exposed new dangers. The lights of cities draw night migrants off course, and many collide with buildings. Some studies also suggest that weak radio signals from electrical equipment can disturb the magnetic compass of robins, although this result has proved hard to reproduce. Researchers hope that a better understanding of how birds find their way will help them to protect the routes on which so many species depend.

passages.title: The rise and fall of the telegraph
paras: A  Before the nineteenth century, information could travel no faster than the person, horse or ship that carried it. A letter from one side of an ocean to the other took weeks, and a general's orders could be out of date before they arrived. Semaphore towers, chains of hilltop stations that signalled with moving arms, were a partial answer, but they worked only in clear weather and only over short distances. The electric telegraph changed everything by separating the message from the messenger. Within a single generation, wires linked most major cities, and before the century ended, cables had joined every inhabited continent. Then, in the space of a few decades, the technology that had seemed a marvel became an antique.

B  Practical telegraphs appeared in the 1830s and 1840s, almost simultaneously in Britain and the United States. The inventors had worked independently, and their machines were quite different: some pointed needles at letters on a dial, while others made marks on moving paper. Sending every letter on a separate wire was far too costly, so the successful systems used a single wire and a code of short and long signals. Once the code was agreed, the system spread rapidly. Operators became so practised that they no longer needed to look at the paper tape; they simply listened to the clicks of the machine and wrote the message as it arrived. A system that began with competing designs soon settled on one standard that all could use.

C  The first customers were the railways, which had a serious problem. Most lines had only a single track, and the only protection against head-on collisions was a rigid timetable. A delayed train could throw the whole schedule into confusion. With a telegraph wire strung along the track, a station could tell the next one that a train had passed, and a dispatcher could change the orders of a train that was already moving. Accidents fell, and the railways quickly came to depend on the new technology. Because the wires already ran to every station, the companies found it easy to let the public send messages from the ticket office, and in this way the telegraph moved from the railway industry into everyday life.

D  Businesses and newspapers soon followed. Merchants could learn the price of cotton or wheat in a distant city on the day it was set, rather than weeks later. Economists have argued that the effect was dramatic: within a decade of a city being connected, the difference between its prices and those in neighbouring markets narrowed sharply, because traders could no longer exploit ignorance. Newspapers, meanwhile, formed agencies that shared the cost of sending reports by wire. Since every word had to be paid for, writers learned to be brief, and the clipped, factual style of the news report owes a great deal to the telegraph. The habit of a headline summing up the story has the same origin.

E  The greatest challenge was the sea. Engineers had to insulate a cable so that the current would not leak away, and they had to make it strong enough to be lowered thousands of metres to the ocean floor. The first Atlantic cable, laid in 1858, carried messages for only a few weeks before it failed, largely because the operators applied too much voltage in an attempt to speed up the signals. A second attempt succeeded in 1866, and a message that would have taken ten days by ship now arrived in minutes. Yet the price was extreme. A short message could cost as much as a labourer earned in several weeks, so the cables were used almost exclusively by governments, banks and large companies. Empires, in particular, valued them as a way of controlling distant territories.

F  The telegraph also created new kinds of work. Messenger boys ran between offices and the homes of recipients, and thousands of operators were employed, many of them women, who were paid less than men for the same skills. Friendships and even marriages began between operators who had never met, and writers of the time spoke of a 'Victorian internet'. There were fears as well. Critics warned that the flood of news would leave people anxious and unable to concentrate, and that rumours would now spread faster than they could be corrected. Criminals soon found ways to send false messages to manipulate the markets, and the first cases of telegraph fraud came to court. Many of the worries we hold today about the speed of information were first expressed in this period.

G  The decline began in the late nineteenth century, with the arrival of the telephone, which carried the human voice directly and needed no trained operator. For a time, the two systems existed side by side, with the telegram surviving because many households had no telephone. As telephones spread and prices fell, however, the telegram was reduced to a special occasion, kept mainly for greetings at weddings and birthdays. Later technologies, including the fax and, finally, electronic mail, removed most of what remained. In the early twenty-first century, one of the largest telegraph services in the world sent its last message. Yet the telegraph has not vanished entirely. The undersea routes it opened are still used by the fibre-optic cables that carry the internet, and the idea of a single worldwide network was one that the telegraph made possible.

passages.title: Is boredom good for us?
paras: A  Boredom has a poor reputation. Parents treat it as a problem to be solved with a screen or an activity; employers regard it as a sign of poor motivation; teachers worry that a bored pupil is a pupil who has stopped learning. The standard assumption is that a bored mind is an idle mind, and that an idle mind is wasting its time. Yet a growing number of psychologists argue that this picture is incomplete. Boredom, they suggest, is a signal, rather like hunger or thirst. It tells us that what we are doing is no longer worth our attention and prompts us to look for something else, and a creature that never felt bored would stay with unrewarding tasks for far too long. I shall argue in this essay that boredom is useful, though not in the simple way its more enthusiastic defenders claim.

B  The best-known evidence for the usefulness of boredom comes from a study carried out at Harrowfield University. Volunteers were asked to spend fifteen minutes copying numbers out of a telephone directory, a task chosen for being as dull as possible. They were then asked to think of as many uses as they could for a plastic cup. Those who had copied numbers produced more ideas, and more unusual ones, than a control group who had gone straight to the cup. The researchers' interpretation was that, with nothing to hold their attention, the bored volunteers let their minds wander, and wandering minds make connections that focused ones miss.

C  It is an appealing story, and it has been repeated in countless magazine articles. It deserves more caution than it usually gets. Several later teams have struggled to replicate the finding, and where they have succeeded, the effect has been modest. Creativity is hard to measure, and a count of ideas about a plastic cup is a very crude test. Anyone who claims that a dull afternoon will turn them into a novelist is therefore claiming too much. What the research does show, in my view, is something less dramatic but still valuable: that when outside demands are removed, the mind does not switch off but turns to a different kind of work.

D  That work has been studied by neuroscientists, who have found that a network of brain regions becomes more active when we are not concentrating on a task. This network appears to be involved in remembering the past, imagining the future and thinking about other people's feelings. In other words, the apparently idle mind is busy with planning and with making sense of experience. These are activities that matter a great deal but rarely feel urgent, so in a busy life they are the first to be pushed aside. Boredom may be the price we pay for being made to attend to them. It is worth noting, too, that the network is not the preserve of the gifted. It is active in everyone, and it can be exercised in much the way that a muscle can.

E  Not all boredom is helpful, and this is where the defenders of the idea often lose their way. Psychologists distinguish between the mild, passing boredom of a queue and the chronic boredom that comes from feeling that nothing one does has any meaning. The latter is linked to low mood, to risk-taking and to a sense of drift, and nobody should be asked to endure it for the sake of creativity. The useful kind is the first: short, safe, and followed by the freedom to choose what to do next. A child who is bored for an hour on a rainy Saturday is in a very different position from an employee who spends years in a job that offers no challenge, and to speak of the two as if they were the same is to confuse the argument.

F  The usual villain in discussions of this subject is the smartphone, which makes it possible to eliminate every moment of boredom. Some commentators have called for the devices to be banned from schools and public places. I find this unconvincing. Bans treat the symptom, and they overlook the fact that people were filling every spare minute with newspapers, cigarettes and chatter long before the phone was invented. A more useful question is not what we reach for but whether we ever leave a gap long enough for the mind to turn inwards. That is a matter of habit, and habits can be changed without legislation. It would be a mistake, too, to assume that earlier generations were more patient than ours. I am aware of no evidence either way, and I suspect the claim says more about nostalgia than about attention.

G  What would it mean to take boredom seriously? For schools, it would mean resisting the urge to fill every minute of the timetable with structured activity, and accepting that a child who complains of having nothing to do is not necessarily being failed. For workplaces, it might mean protecting stretches of time without meetings or messages. And for individuals, it means treating the first twinge of boredom not as an emergency but as an invitation: to daydream, to notice, or to pick something up for its own sake. None of this guarantees a flash of genius. But a mind that is never given any space to wander cannot, by definition, wander somewhere new.
